summary: At nearly 95 square miles, Palm Springs sprawls across more land than San Francisco yet holds fewer than 45,000 residents — a density of just 473 people per square mile that means long, empty stretches of desert floor between pockets of development, all hemmed in by the dramatic vertical wall of the San Jacinto Mountains rising over 10,000 feet to the west. That western escarpment delivers reliable alpenglow sunsets, and the Palm Springs Aerial Tramway — the world's largest rotating tramcar — climbs from desert heat to alpine forest in ten minutes, a genuine geographic oddity. Summer daily highs routinely exceed 100°F for months, which makes the 10.4 hours of average daily sunshine a double-edged gift; winter, by contrast, is strikingly mild and bright, essentially the economic engine of the city, since tourism, hospitality, and the service sector dominate local employment rather than any single large corporate campus. A home-price-to-income ratio near 7.9× and a rent-to-income ratio around 24.5% means purchasing is a stretch at the median income while renting remains technically within conventional affordability thresholds. Property crime runs high at 3,722 per 100,000, with larceny alone at 2,587 — worth weighing against the fact that a large share of housing sits vacant part of the year. Palm Springs is fundamentally a place whose economy and rhythm are shaped by seasonal migration, which means its restaurants, galleries along Palm Canyon Drive, and mid-century architectural identity pulse with energy for half the year and grow conspicuously quiet for the other half.
